Unknown operation keys, nested unresolved arguments, callable results and even
known-lambda applications retain their stated unknown cases. An unopened
lambda capture can still lose its bound name through the runtime dependency
projection, so this analyzer cannot replace template checking before opening.

The analogous [builtin-read Ash fixture](fixtures/copied-integer-cell-result.ash)
passes current Core elaboration and execution, returning `41 : Int` when the
copied-value closure is called after its owner closes. This supplies another
concrete result comparison, not an authenticated Core translation or simulation.

One checked counterexample fixes a requirement for signature-aware preservation.
The raw capture relation permits choosing a saved input annotation
independently of the operation's declared result. For a typed integer-producing
request, choosing a reference input can invalidate the saved return check even
though the pre-state is typed and passes the finite result check. The earlier
all-raw-step theorem could weaken an unknown request result to any saved input
bound; that argument no longer applies to a finite request result. Signature
agreement must constrain the capture annotation, or execution must use the
existing signature-derived typed capture constructor. This is a condition on
the experiment's checked execution relation, not evidence of a Core defect.

The following module proves local preservation of these return checks across
every raw transition under signature agreement and allocation premises. Its
connection to template checking and general calculus admission, and formal Core
correspondence remain open. A finite inferred normal-result bound does not
establish normal termination, operation-payload safety or disposal readiness.

## Signature-aware return-check preservation

[OperationReturns.lean](OperationReturns.lean) threads the signature-aware
analyzer through actual plain frames, active stacks and saved continuations.
`Checked` recursively checks each cell's normal-return bound. A live ticket
checks its saved stack at the bound of its declared input port and its outside
stack at unknown. The new frame and stack observers retain the previous
conservative treatment of control results. They are observers of the existing
execution grammar, not new computations or bind operators.

`CaptureInput` checks one event's request, created owner and saved input
annotation. For the singleton ticket creation used by raw capture, it requires
an actual decoded operation key, its exact signature lookup, the matching live
owner and equality of the saved input's erased port to the declared result.
Other creation shapes impose no condition here; the actual `RawStep`
constructors establish which events can create tickets. Equal storage bounds
are insufficient: `Unit` and `Int` both have scalar bounds but remain different
ports. Checked negative examples reject both a reference annotation for an
integer-producing operation and this scalar-to-scalar mismatch.

`raw_step_preserves_checked` covers every actual raw transition. Its premises
are current value-type checking under `withCellSignatures users`, current return
checks, `CaptureInput`, and a local `AllocationReturn` certificate for any new
cell. It concludes the successor's return checks. Fixed builtin signatures
justify read and write result bounds; an arbitrary supplied signature cannot
replace them in this theorem. Capture uses signature agreement to retain the
saved bound. Resume uses current typing and the historical ticket table to
bound the actual operand. Ordinary bind uses closed-value support substitution.
Discard materialization generates Unit-returning release frames. Frame and
stack recomposition preserve the remaining checks in each case.

The theorem neither assumes nor proves arbitrary raw successor typing. It does
not establish future allocation certificates, payload safety, disposal
readiness or general admission. In particular, its allocation certificate uses
the new runtime analyzer on the actual opened body. The
[declaration-derived template checker](#declaration-derived-template-entry) below
now supplies that certificate for the existing resource-parameter declaration
fragment; general execution admission remains separate.

`typed_capture_constructs_checked` starts with the current request's return
check and derives the bound required by the saved stack. It constructs one
actual capture event, its signature agreement, a historical ticket-table
extension, and the same successor's typing and return checks. Freshness here
means absence from that type table; issued-owner freshness, access and closing
conditions remain independent. `typed_resume_constructs_checked` similarly
constructs the actual resume event with both successor typing and return
checks.

For current values, `typed_cell_return_excludes` derives absence of the closing
identity from actual storage or a canonical first-order port. Value transitions
need neither a new allocation certificate nor a capture-annotation choice.
`checked_value_progress` and `checked_ready_value_progress` pair this new
return invariant with the existing joint validity or readiness judgment,
preserving both for the same actual named step. These are current-value
progress theorems, not progress throughout execution from an initial calculus
term.

The integer-producing handler example now passes return checking at the
pending request as well as after actual capture and resume. The builtin-read
example crosses a binding frame above its cell and preserves the whole stack's
return checks. That example proves an actual read event and those checks; it
does not establish a complete typed, live, freshly issued execution or final
release. The earlier Ash fixtures remain observable comparisons rather than
formal Core correspondence. Signature agreement repairs the experiment's
unchecked raw annotation choice; it supplies no evidence that Core violates
its current specification.

## Declaration-derived template entry

[DeclarationResults.lean](DeclarationResults.lean) reuses the existing
`FamilyTemplate`, `FamilyValid`, `checkFamily` and `parameterEnvironment` from
[declaration signatures](DeclaredSignatures.lean). It extends positional
resource-parameter binding to `ResourceName`: a formal parameter may receive
an unresolved lexical resource name or an actual activation. `namedParameters`
rejects wrong arity and non-resource arguments. Its opening theorem transports
those exact ordered bindings, including repeated actual arguments. It does not
flatten or deduplicate resource occurrences within general type arguments.

This remains the existing resource-parameter fragment. `FamilyValid` checks
distinct formal parameters, a nonempty operation vector and the scope of every
resource name in both input and output metadata. It is not Core's full kind,
module-provenance, visibility or declaration authentication. General nominal
and applied type arguments remain outside this parameter-binding model. The
current specification's ordered declaration substitution motivates the bridge;
this experiment supplies neither its full elaborator nor a Core translation.

`typeBound` reads stored-result support from the declared output: scalar ports
have empty support, references retain their substituted resource names, products
combine their bounds, and functions remain unknown. Function input/output,
latent-row and retained metadata still participate in whole-declaration
validation and structural type realization. Erasing to the existing `Port`
representation does not turn function declarations into capture bounds.

The source `operationBound` validates the family, selects the actual operation
position, binds its resource arguments and then reads the output bound.
`operation_bound_open` proves that this process commutes with resource opening.
`userSignature` compiles the same declaration through existing `ValueType`
instantiation and type decoding. `signature` adds the fixed builtin cell
signatures. `declared_signature_known` connects this executable lookup to
`DeclaredOperation`; the decoder's frozen and realized-type lemmas justify the
compiled ports. `operation_bound_runtime` proves agreement of source and
runtime result bounds, including failed lookup cases. Validating the entire
declaration is essential: a malformed input cannot be excused by an integer
output. Closed argument/effect lemmas extend the agreement from explicitly
frozen instances to resource-closed metadata.

[DeclarationTemplates.lean](DeclarationTemplates.lean) integrates that operation
case with the existing finite template-support grammar. It keeps free resource
names through actual lambda capture and ordinary binding analysis. Its
`infer_instantiate` and `runtime_agreement` prove transport through opening and
agreement with `OperationResults.analyze` on resource-closed code under the
compiled declaration signature. `check` inspects only this inferred bound and
the supplied resource world. The checker is equivalent to its finite
`SourceBound` certificate; this is completeness for that observer, not a claim
to accept every safe term. `fresh_opening_runtime_iff` relates the initial
body's check to the actual freshly opened body's runtime bound.

`checked_source_entry` constructs the actual raw allocation and the
`OperationReturns.AllocationReturn` certificate for that same opened body.
It requires resource closure and freshness in the supplied world, and imposes
no first-order restriction on the returned value's type. In the named machine,
`resource_named_preserves_checked` obtains freshness from the event's issuance
history and applies the template check to its actual allocated identity.
`checked_resource_entry_progress` combines this result with existing resource
entry progress: the same named step preserves joint validity and the new return
invariant. The initial configuration must already have joint validity and
current return checks. This is a derived resource-entry rule, not complete
admission of arbitrary initial terms or all later transitions.

Positive evidence now includes the copied-read closure template before opening,
its raw entry certificate for every supplied identity, and a concrete typed
initial configuration whose named allocation preserves joint validity and
return checks. Generic declared integer results also flow through bindings into
capture-free closures. A reference-producing declaration preserves the bound
resource name and rejects returning that captured owner; the analogous capture
of a supplied outer resource passes. Negative examples cover a retained reader,
unopened captures, callable results, unknown calls, malformed input metadata,
duplicate or undeclared formal parameters, runtime atoms in declarations,
missing families/operations, and wrong argument shapes. Aliased actual resource
arguments remain accepted. The concrete joint example establishes one fresh
entry step, not its complete execution or final release.

The [ordinary-substitution result](#declaration-template-substitution) below
now preserves this checker for later resource bodies under structural
closed-value binding certificates. Known-call result summaries, future
capture/payload/closing admission, general progress
throughout execution and Core simulation also remain open. The earlier
ordinary-substitution proofs use the previous analyzer; the next module supplies
the required bridge through actual closed-value storage. No Core or normative
language change follows from this
experimental declaration and template integration.

## Declaration-template substitution

[DeclarationSubstitution.lean](DeclarationSubstitution.lean) preserves the
new declaration-derived template checker under ordinary closed-value
substitution. It reuses `TemplateSubstitution.BindingsChecked`, `replaceAll`
and the grammar-only closure/opening lemmas. `closed_value_bound_iff` proves
that the old and signature-aware analyzers give the same bound for an actual
closed value. This justifies reusing the existing structural binding
certificate; it does not equate the analyzers on pending computations or
unfold known calls.

`substitution_below` uses the signature-aware support-substitution and
environment-monotonicity lemmas. A replacement value must be resource-closed,
closed over ordinary variables and tickets, and lie within its variable's
stored-support bound. `replacements_below` composes these checks in the existing
replacement order under the same ordinary environment. Duplicate variable
names retain the existing sequential replacement behavior; the list operation
is code substitution, not evaluation of a list of nested bindings.

`opened_replacements_bound` transports a checked template through actual
opening and replacement. `source_bound_replacements` reflects this result back
to the original finite template checker. Its fresh-number witness is chosen
outside the supplied world only for the proof; it does not choose an issued
runtime identity. `checked_replacements_preserve_check` therefore concludes
that the same checker succeeds on the substituted resource body. These results
require resource closure of the enclosing resource expression. They do not
supply a general admission judgment for all nested lexical resource contexts.

`checked_replaced_entry` derives the new body's local allocation-return
certificate and its actual raw entry. `bind_then_entry` connects an actual
strict bind to that same substituted entry, with ordinary closure and world
freshness explicit. The stronger `checked_bind_resource_progress` starts with
current joint validity, current return checks, an actual value initializer,
its support bound in the analysis environment, and the earlier template check.
Current typing supplies the bind's `ClosedValue`, `ClosedExcept` and
resource-closure premises through `typed_bind_ready`.

The stronger theorem constructs two actual named steps. The bind preserves
issuance and activation histories, and its resulting configuration is exactly
the resource expression with the substituted body. Both its result and the
following fresh allocation preserve joint validity and return checks. The
declaration signature stays fixed. The bind leaves the template-check world
unchanged, and allocation extends the runtime typing world. The
intermediate expression is a resource expression, whose result observer is
unknown; inheriting its outer return checks does not establish the new cell's
bound. The preserved template check supplies that separate bound at entry.

The concrete example binds `17` to an ordinary variable, then enters a cell
initialized to `41`. Its body will read the cell and return a closure retaining
the ordinary variable and the copied read result. The earlier template passes
the new checker while the old analyzer reports unknown. Substitution preserves
the new check, and an actual typed initial configuration exercises both joined
steps. This evidence establishes the bind and fresh entry, not the subsequent
read, closure return or final release.

Other examples show that a typed integer supplies the same binding certificate,
a function retaining a resource allowed by the supplied outer world can be
substituted, and a function with an uncertified hidden handle breaks a scalar
bound and the template check. The outer-function example checks support and
substitution only; it does not independently prove that the supplied outer
resource is live. Identity-free function ports cannot replace these stored
support checks.

This closes ordinary-substitution preservation for the new local template
checker under its stated closure and binding premises. Inferring bounds for
arbitrary pending bindings, admitting all nested resource templates, preserving
closing readiness through those executions, general initial-term admission and
Core correspondence remain open. The two-step theorem preserves `Valid` and
return checks; it does not claim the stronger `Ready` invariant or general
whole-run progress.

Nested admission must preserve lexical shadowing. A saved alias of an outer
resource and a direct reference to an inner resource can use the same source
binder numeral while denoting different acquisitions. The following transport
construction preserves that distinction once the outer aliases have been
resolved. Deriving those environments recursively from an initial calculus
term remains open.

## Symbolic template worlds and shadowing

[SymbolicTemplates.lean](SymbolicTemplates.lean) reuses declaration-template
inference and the existing lexical opening operation. Its `check` asks whether
the inferred resource-name list is contained in a supplied symbolic world.
`check_iff_bound` characterizes that finite check, and `check_world_mono`
permits enlarging the world. This check alone is not an initial-term admission
judgment: the supplied names must denote the right acquisitions.

`snapshot` opens an ordinary support environment's resource names with the
current resource environment. `check_transport` opens code, support metadata
and the symbolic world together. `realized_check` connects this transported
check to the existing runtime template checker when the world has structural
`ListRealizes` evidence and the snapshotted support environment equals the
runtime support environment. `realized_check_in_world` permits the realized
world to be a subset of the target world. Distinct symbolic names may alias the
same acquisition; the realized list may contain duplicates and need not
mention every issued resource. Neither support equality nor list realization
proves that actual lexical values satisfy those bounds or that the resources
are live.

`snapshot_binding` shows that extending an ordinary environment with an
initializer's inferred bound commutes with opening that initializer. A fully
realized snapshot is unchanged by later openings, through
`realized_snapshot_stable`; this follows from activation identities being
stable under opening. It is not commutation of arbitrary resource environments.
Unresolved names can still change, and an unknown support bound remains unknown.

The resource constructor opens its initializer in the outer environment and
its body in the environment masked at the new binder. The new
`symbolic_entry_certificate` follows that actual constructor, using realization
under the masked environment for its body check. Saved outer aliases must
already record their outer identities before this masking boundary. The
certificate supplies an actual raw entry and the opened body's allocation-return
bound. `symbolic_resource_entry_progress` additionally starts with current joint
validity and return checks. It allows the realized symbolic world to be included
in the actual issued-resource world, then constructs the same named entry with
joint validity and return checks preserved. Issuance freshness and live-support
evidence come from the existing execution judgments, not from symbolic membership.

The shadowing examples use outer identity `8` and inner identity `9`, both
introduced using lexical binder numeral `4`. Ordinary variable `3` retains the
outer resource. Snapshotting its support records activation `8`; opening the
inner body changes its direct reference to activation `9` while preserving the
saved alias. A closure retaining only the saved outer alias passes the inner
return check; a closure retaining the direct inner reference fails. Checking
both against the unsnapshotted singleton world `[bound 4]` would accept both.
The examples prove that this world cannot realize under the masked body
environment, and that a single lexical name cannot realize to both distinct
acquisitions in one environment.

Other examples check initializer/body scope separation, unchanged unknown
bounds, noninjective aliases, and weakening from a duplicate realized world to
a larger issued world. The raw alias-entry example still contains an ordinary
variable and establishes only its stated local certificate. A separate example
checks an actual closed function retaining `8` against the saved support bound,
then proves an actual bind followed by entry of the substituted body at `9` with
its allocation-return certificate. These raw examples do not supply an initial
outer acquisition, a valid enclosing stack, or subsequent return/release steps.

This completes the symbolic-world transport and snapshot bridge for local
entry. A recursive initial-term judgment must still construct the appropriate
lexical environments and value certificates at every nested scope, derive
pending computation bounds and closing readiness, and preserve these through
whole executions. General progress and formal correspondence with current Core
remain open. The module adds no computation model or sequencing operator.

## Generative result derivations

[GenerativeResults.lean](GenerativeResults.lean) adds a structural finite
result-support judgment over the existing `Code` grammar. It addresses a
specific limitation of `DeclarationTemplates.infer`: a resource expression
currently has unknown support, even when its nested body returns a known
resource-free closure. This prevents an outer scope from inheriting that known
result through the old observer.

`Derives declarations environment world code bound` records an outward stored
support bound. Its leaves use the existing finite template check, restricted
to values and ordinary variables. Separate pair, bind, branch and operation
constructors retain derivations for their strict children. A bind checks its
body with the initializer's finite bound installed in the ordinary support
environment. `summary` represents that bound as resource products with a scalar
terminator; `summary_support` proves the represented list exactly. This summary
contains no callable-behavior information.

The resource constructor checks the initializer and resource-name closure of
the whole expression. For every identity outside the current world, it requires
a recursive derivation for the body opened at that identity, in the extended
world. Every such derivation uses the same outward bound, which must be
contained in the original world. These premises inspect the syntactically
opened body; they do not assume a future execution step or a successor invariant.
The rule is declarative. Its quantification over fresh identities is not a
claimed finite decision procedure.

`resource_closed` derives source-name closure from this judgment.
`value_support` proves that an actual closed value's stored resource dependencies
lie in its derived bound. `substitution` preserves the whole derivation when an
actual closed replacement satisfies its ordinary environment bound. In the
resource case, substitution commutes with the existing fresh opening; in the
bind case, an ordinary binder that shadows the substituted variable masks the
body replacement. `world_mono` transports derivations to larger worlds without
requiring resource aliases to be injective.

`value_below_summary` derives the initializer value's bound from its structural
derivation and actual closed-value support. `bind_value_derivation` then
preserves the suffix derivation after substitution, retaining the justified
extended analysis environment. `bind_preserves_spine_and_joint` derives the
ordinary closure premises from current typing and constructs the same named
bind step with joint validity and the cell-spine certificate preserved. It does
not require a separately supplied replacement-support bound. The current
computation's analysis environment changes; surrounding ordinary continuations
will need to retain their own environments when that certificate is extended.

`resource_entry` constructs the actual raw entry, exposes the recursively
checked opened body, and proves that its fresh identity is absent from the
outward bound. That expression result alone is insufficient for general stack
preservation: the older `OperationReturns.frameResult` maps a cell frame to
unknown. The new `CellSpine` certificate retains one unchanged outward bound
through a consecutive spine of actual cell frames. Each frame excludes its
owner from that bound. `resource_entry_preserves_spine` pushes the certificate
with the actual new frame. `cell_return_preserves_spine` derives the return's
actual access checks and retains the certificate on the remaining spine.
`cell_return_preserves_joint` additionally preserves existing joint validity
for that same value-return event.

The concrete example uses two nested resource declarations with the same
lexical binder numeral `4`. They acquire identities `8` and `9`, then return a
constant closure. The old observer reports unknown for the inner resource
expression; the recursive judgment derives the empty bound for both resource
expressions. The example proves its initial term typed and jointly valid,
follows the two actual entries and two returns with their result/spine
certificates, and proves the whole run preserves the ownership ledger with no
duplicate completion. The events release inner `9` before outer `8`; the ledger
stores completion history newest-first, so its final list is `[8,9]`.
This is not an all-transition joint-validity theorem for arbitrary derivations.

A second derivation retains a pending ordinary variable through both resource
bodies. Certified substitution of `17` preserves that recursive derivation, and
an actual preceding bind joins the same nested raw trace. A typed, jointly
valid starting bind also exercises the joined theorem and derives its own
replacement-support bound. A negative example
binds an unsafe resource result and then ignores it. The old final-result check
reports empty support, but `Derives` rejects the term because the initializer
would return its own acquisition. This demonstrates why arbitrary finite-check
leaves cannot replace recursive checking of strict children.

The [nested-resource Core fixture](fixtures/nested-resource-closure-result.ash)
returns `17 : Int`. It returns a closure through both resource scopes and calls
that closure afterward. The Lean nested trace ends at the returned closure;
a separate checked beta step applies it and obtains `17`. This is comparison
evidence, not an authenticated Core translation or simulation proof. The
observer's unknown result is classified as a proof-model precision limitation,
not a Core defect or a proposed language change: the current
[resource-dependency rules](../../../../spec/static-semantics.md#scoped-cells-and-resource-dependencies)
permit closures with no dependency on either closing acquisition to leave
those scopes.

`Derives` checks result support independently of value types. It does not, for
example, enforce that a cell initializer has type `Int`; the existing typing
judgment supplies that requirement. Lambda leaves check stored captures without
checking future execution of their bodies. Applications, handlers, resumptions,
discard and cleanup have no finite-result constructors here. Ordinary-frame
transport, handler forests, capture/resume of these new certificates, closing
readiness and whole-run progress remain open. The current value-bind rule
retains its extended analysis environment rather than assuming that the
eliminated variable's entry can be removed. Connecting that environment to
ordinary continuation frames and their result transformations remains required.
The module therefore strengthens the result-support component of initial-term
admission without claiming to finish that admission judgment.

## Generative results through frames and captures

[GenerativeFrames.lean](GenerativeFrames.lean) transports the recursive result
judgment through ordinary evaluation contexts and actual saved control forests.
Each plain frame keeps its own analysis environment. When an initializer bind
extends the current environment, it does not replace the environment saved by
an enclosing waiting bind. `returned_value_rebind` transfers an actual closed
value's support derivation to the saved environment; it does not assert that
the two environments give equivalent meanings to arbitrary open code.

`ContextReturns` relates a context's input support bound to its output bound.
Its pair, bind, branch, operation and resource cases retain the recursive
premises from `Derives`. `focus_decompose` extracts a child derivation and a
matching context certificate from every actual focus of a supported expression.
`context_plug` reconstructs the whole derivation. In particular, an enclosing
bind that ignores its initializer still requires the initializer's derivation.
`context_plug_returned_value` performs this reconstruction using the waiting
frame's environment after an actual value returns.

`StackReturns` composes these transformations in control order. A cell passes
its input bound only when that bound excludes its owner. A handler frame passes
a normal result; that constructor supplies no premise about its clauses.
A live ticket retains a separate certificate for its saved capture and another
for its active tail. `stack_append` composes matching bounds, while
`stack_decompose` extracts their shared intermediate bound. Both preserve the
saved capture when extending a live ticket's active tail. The old consecutive
cell-spine certificate embeds into this judgment, and all these certificates
transport to larger worlds.

`capture_certificate` uses the actual `HandlerCut` decomposition to preserve
the captured forest's result certificate and construct the new live boundary's
certificate. The selected clause still needs its own result derivation at the
exposed answer bound. This theorem neither checks that clause nor proves that
the new active expression satisfies `ConfigurationReturns`.

For resumption, `ResumeBound` obtains a finite support bound from the actual
saved input port. `resumed_value_derivation` uses historical ticket typing to
check the value against that port. Its typing signature is compiled from the
same declaration registry used by the result derivations. The saved capture's
output bound must also match the input bound of the active prefix that will
follow it. `resume_recomposition` and `resume_step` take that compatibility as
an explicit premise and restore the actual capture before that prefix and the
spent ticket. The latter constructs the raw resume event, including the ticket
discharge, and proves the resulting configuration's support certificate.
Exact bound equality is the sufficient composition discipline proved here;
the module does not claim it is necessary when a containment rule could suffice.

Neither a bare live-ticket certificate nor equality of value types establishes
this result-bound compatibility. A checked negative example types a function
that retains resource `8` at an identity-free function port but rejects an empty
stored-support bound for the value. Callable input ports still have unknown
support in `ResumeBound`. Supporting such one-shot inputs requires additional
value-support information; it is not deferred to multishot continuations.

`ConfigurationReturns` pairs the current computation's derivation with its
stack transformation. Local theorems preserve it through actual focus, plugging,
value binding, fresh resource entry, cell return and normal handler return.
Cell return also derives the actual access checks. The result judgment remains
independent of typing, ownership and closing readiness; these local statements
do not constitute preservation of the full joint invariant.

The ordinary-frame example places a nested-resource initializer inside a
waiting bind. A second bind with the same ordinary name extends the current
analysis environment while the waiting frame retains its original environment.
The example proves its initial typing and joint validity, then checks eight
actual steps with result certificates: focus, inner bind, two entries, two
returns, plugging and the final bind. Its execution preserves the ownership
ledger and releases inner `9` before outer `8`. A capture example checks a
saved ordinary frame and resource owner, then reconstructs an actual resumed
configuration under a declaration-compiled signature. A separate nonempty-prefix
example composes an empty saved result into an outer-resource-retaining result,
then drops that dependency before the outer owner closes. This last example
checks certificate composition, not a typed execution of the whole configuration.

The [ordinary-bind Core fixture](fixtures/nested-resource-bind-result.ash)
returns `17 : Int` after a closure passes through both resource scopes and the
waiting bind. As in the preceding fixture, Lean's trace ends at the closure;
its application is checked separately in `GenerativeResults`. The Core run is
comparison evidence, not formal correspondence. No Core or specification change
is required by this example.

This completes a local transport component for normal results and saved
captures. It does not finish an initial-program judgment. Applications and
clause-result checking, actual request payload bounds, capture-specific closing
certificates, and armed or running cleanup frames still require integration.
The module deliberately has no generic cleanup-frame pass-through rule.
Deriving all later checks from an initial term, proving progress throughout
execution, and formal Core correspondence remain open. Multishot, escaping
continuations and suspension are outside the current target.

## Generative results joined with current progress

[GenerativeProgress.lean](GenerativeProgress.lean) joins the recursive result
certificates with the existing scoped `Ready` judgment. `Ready` contains the
joint typing, effect, usage, ownership, naming and live-support invariant,
plus historical closing interfaces. The new join derives the current access
checks from result evidence instead of requesting them as an additional premise.
It does not establish the admission conditions for a later handler clause.

`NoSourceRequest` marks an explicit local boundary. It says that a current
operation with a value operand has no source-handler `HandlerCut` in the actual
stack. Its definition examines syntax and ordered interpretation; it contains
no execution witness or successor invariant. Non-request expressions and
values satisfy it. An actual builtin `CellUpdate` supplies it because builtin
selection excludes a source cut. This includes the existing blocking rule:
a source handler overriding the same cell instance is a source-handler boundary,
not a builtin case. Outward requests remain possible observations.

`return_access_checks` uses the actual closed returned value and the top cell's
excluded support bound to discharge release checking. A source capture is
excluded by the local boundary. Discard is excluded by the current expression's
`Derives` judgment. This is not a new disposal-admission rule. `SupportedHead`
records the outer forms represented by `Derives`; it does not inspect latent
function bodies or add new syntax.

`raw_preserves_results` covers every raw transition compatible with the current
result certificate and boundary. Focus, plugging, binding and normal returns
use the preceding frame theorems. Branch selection retains the selected child's
derivation. Cell updates preserve the actual stack's result transformation;
builtin reads and writes produce resource-free scalar results. Resource entry
uses the actual issued-owner freshness check to obtain an identity outside
`resourceWorld issued`, then transports the remaining stack to the extended
world. Spent-ticket return retains the tail certificate. Unsupported expression
or cleanup-frame cases are impossible by inversion of `Derives` or
`StackReturns`. Source capture contradicts `NoSourceRequest`.

This raw theorem preserves only result evidence; arbitrary raw annotations do
not establish joint typing. `current_progress` uses the existing typed progress
construction to choose the annotations of the same actual next step. It derives
access checks, preserves the result certificate, and retains closing interfaces.
The boundary ensures that no new ticket is allocated, so registry history and
extension imply that the historical registry is unchanged. The conclusion is
a terminal value, an outward request, or that step together with both `Ready`
and `ConfigurationReturns`. Resource allocation can still enlarge the world.
All typing in the join uses the signature compiled from the same declarations
as the result judgment.

`nonrequest_progress`, `value_progress` and `closed_progress` specialize this
join. In particular, current value progress needs no separate access-check or
request-boundary premise. `initial_progress` starts from independent expression
typing, one-shot usage, absence of initial stored resource atoms, and a result
derivation under the unknown ordinary environment. Empty control establishes
the initial boundary and closing interfaces. This proves the first step with
both certificates; it does not prove that these initial checks suffice for all
later steps.

The examples exercise an ordinary initial bind and an actual builtin read.
Two negative checks explain the remaining premises. Reusing an already issued
resource identity permits a raw entry whose successor has no result certificate;
this shows why issued-history freshness cannot be dropped. Separately, plugging
a returned operand exposes a ready source request: the raw step preserves the
result certificate while `NoSourceRequest` becomes false. This is a concrete
raw/result-certificate example, not an asserted full jointly valid execution.
It rules out treating the boundary as automatically preserved.

The existing [copied-cell Core fixture](fixtures/copied-integer-cell-result.ash)
returns `41 : Int`. The Lean read produces the copied integer while preserving
the waiting continuation's result certificate. This remains concrete comparison
evidence, not a formal Core simulation.

The join covers the supported normal forms and builtin requests. It does not
add application, handler installation, resume, discard or cleanup constructors
to `Derives`. Ready source requests still need clause-result and payload
admission, and callable support and cleanup require their own integration.
The boundary must not be used to discard those obligations from the one-shot
target. Whole-execution progress and formal Core correspondence remain open.

## Lexical continuation results and clause checking

[ClauseResults.lean](ClauseResults.lean) adds structural clause-result checking
to the same `Code` grammar. It introduces no computation model, bind operation
or machine transition. The generalized `Derives` judgment embeds the preceding
`GenerativeResults.Derives` as an existing fragment and adds recursive result
rules for expressions containing handlers and resumptions. Its `TicketBound`
index is either absent or records a lexical continuation binder, an input
support bound and an answer support bound. This is result information, not
permission to use a continuation.

A resume checks its operand against the matching lexical ticket's input bound
and has that ticket's answer bound. A handler checks its handled body at an
outward bound `R`. The mutually defined `ClausesDerive` checks every clause at
that same `R`, installing a new lexical ticket for each clause. The handled
body retains its surrounding ticket contract; a nested clause receives its own.
Thus `R` is a shared upper bound for both normal body completion and final
clause completion. The actual saved output and waiting prefix must still agree
when a resume is executed; the lexical contract does not establish that stack
compatibility by itself.

Each clause checks against the same compiled operation declaration used by
port typing. The finite support of the operation's input port supplies the
ordinary parameter bound; the finite support of its output port supplies the
continuation input bound. Callable ports remain unknown here. They need
additional actual-value support contracts within the one-shot target. Coverage,
unique operation keys, value types and one-shot use remain separate checks;
a clause-result derivation does not supply them.

`resource_closed` derives resource-name closure. Actual closed values recover
a derivation in the existing result fragment, so `value_support` bounds their
stored dependencies. World transport and certified ordinary substitution are
proved for both expressions and clause lists. Ordinary binders mask substitution
in their own bodies; clause parameters do the same. The lexical ticket contract
is unchanged by ordinary substitution. Resource cases use the existing
commutation theorem for closed-value substitution and fresh body opening,
preserving previously recorded activation identities.

`selected_clause` retrieves the result derivation for an actual `ClauseAt`.
`selected_clause_substitution` first equates the selected declaration lookup
with the actual operand's operation lookup, then derives the operand's finite
support from its typing. It substitutes that operand into the actual selected
body while retaining the justified parameter environment and lexical ticket.
This does not prove that the operand may cross the captured resource owners;
outward payload access remains an independent obligation.

`HandlerResults` retains these derivations for the actual runtime handler and
its chosen answer bound. The older handler-frame pass-through certificate
cannot recover this information. `capture_result` combines the retained clause
check, an actual typed request, exact handler cut, selected clause and saved/tail
result interfaces. It constructs the raw capture, derives the active clause's
result bound after parameter substitution, and constructs the live boundary's
existing stack-result certificate. It does not establish fresh ticket allocation,
payload access, successor typing, usage or joint validity for that event.

`resume_result` checks a current resume under the lexical result contract.
Current typing supplies actual value closure; the source-derived operand
certificate supplies its support bound. The saved capture's output must equal
the actual active prefix's input. The theorem constructs the raw resumption,
including ticket discharge, and recovers the existing configuration-result
certificate afterward. This local theorem can use an independently justified
operand support bound without requiring that bound to be inferred from a finite
raw input port. General callable clause admission is still absent.

One example extends the earlier resource-owning capture: the selected clause
now has a checked result derivation, and its actual resume restores the existing
saved-frame certificate. Another example checks a closed handler program
independently for result support, ordinary typing and one-shot usage, deriving
its initial `Ready` state. In its thirteen-step raw execution, the outer clause
resumes its continuation with `42`, continues through a waiting bind, installs an inner handler,
resumes that handler with `17`, and leaves both spent ticket boundaries. The
run proves the ownership ledger with tickets `5` and `6` issued once and consumed
in that order. Completion history is newest-first, so its final list is `[6,5]`.

The inner handler is installed after the outer ticket has been consumed. This
example demonstrates nested source clauses and restored lexical scopes; it
does not demonstrate two simultaneously live continuations or competing active
handler delimiters. Initial readiness plus this raw execution and ledger also
does not prove readiness or result-certificate preservation at every trace state.
The [matching Core fixture](fixtures/nested-handler-clause-result.ash) returns
`17 : Int`, matching the Lean endpoint. This is concrete comparison evidence,
not formal translation or simulation.

Negative checks show that the result judgment can accept two resumptions while
the independent one-shot usage judgment rejects their sequence, that a clause
cannot resume a different lexical binder, and that callable parameter support
does not become finite merely because the callable's port omits retained
resources. These checks preserve the separation between result information,
control permission and actual stored support.

The following retained-frame construction carries the generalized clause
judgment through contexts, handlers and captures. Applications, latent callable
behavior, payload access and cleanup still require integration.
Whole-execution progress and formal Core correspondence remain open; none of
these obligations is replaced by the new result judgment.

## Retained continuation result contracts

[ClauseFrames.lean](ClauseFrames.lean) carries the lexical clause-result
judgments through the existing runtime stack. It retains ordinary environments,
lexical ticket contracts and actual handler clauses. It introduces no expression,
sequencing operation or runtime transition. The question tested here is whether
capture and resumption can derive their result interfaces from structural
certificates, including intervening frames, without an externally supplied
saved-output/prefix-input equality.

`ResultRecord` stores a continuation's input bound `Q` and answer bound `B`.
A historical `Registry` associates that record with its runtime owner.
`ScopeBound` links a runtime lexical scope to the corresponding `TicketBound`.
A record survives consumption so a restored caller scope still has the same
result information. Historical lookup grants no right to resume: one-shot use
and live ownership remain independently checked.

`ContextReturns` checks the actual waiting expression, retaining its ordinary
environment and lexical ticket contract. It includes the existing pair, bind,
branch, operation and resource contexts, plus resume operands. `focus_decompose`
recovers the child and its context from the generalized expression judgment.
`context_plug` reconstructs the expression. For a returned closed value,
`context_plug_returned_value` can change the analysis environment and widen its
support bound, using actual stored dependencies. It does not equate the saved
environment with the child's environment or widen arbitrary computation
judgments. In particular, arbitrary widening would conflict with a resource
expression's requirement that its outward bound lie within the preceding world.

`StackReturns` gives each retained frame an explicit result interface:

| Frame | Required result evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Empty stack | Incoming support is contained in the final bound. |
| Ordinary context | Its saved scope and context are checked; actual incoming support is contained in the context's expected input. |
| Cell | The saved scope is checked and its owner is absent from incoming support; the tail accepts that support. |
| Handler | Actual clauses are checked at one answer bound; incoming support is contained in it and the tail accepts it. |
| Live continuation | The historical record is known, its saved capture maps `Q` to `B`, the caller scope is checked, incoming support is contained in `B`, and the tail accepts `B`. |
| Spent continuation | The same historical answer and caller scope remain; incoming support is contained in `B` and the tail accepts `B`. |

`stack_input_weaken` allows smaller actual input support. The direction is
essential: `I ⊆ E` permits a frame expecting `E` to receive `I`. It does not
permit a capture producing `E` to feed a context accepting only `I`. The saved
context environment, handler answer and continuation record stay fixed.
`stack_append` and `stack_decompose` compose and recover interfaces through the
active tail, preserving dormant captures. Larger resource worlds and extensions
of the historical registry preserve all these certificates.

`handler_cut_certificate` follows the actual ordered `HandlerCut`, including
intervening ordinary, cell, handler, live and spent frames. It recovers the
selected handler's own clause checks, saved scope, answer bound, captured
interface and outside interface. No commutation of handlers is assumed.
`declared_output_included` proves that the operation's canonical finite result
support is contained in the current request's possibly conservative result
bound. It uses the same compiled operation lookup as typing.

`capture_step` combines these facts with actual request typing and selection.
It obtains the selected clause derivation from the stack, substitutes the typed
operand, narrows the captured input to the declared result support, records a
fresh `(Q,B)` pair and constructs the actual raw capture and successor result
certificate. It assumes that the owner is absent from this result registry.
It does not yet derive that absence from the machine's issued-owner history,
prove payload access or construct the successor's full joint invariant.

For `resume_recomposition`, the current lexical scope resolves to a record
`(Q,B)`. The resume expression has bound `B`, and the same owner's live capture
has interface `Q → B`. Decomposing the actual active stack exposes a prefix
`B → M`, with `M ⊆ B` at the live boundary. Replacing that boundary with its
spent form and prepending the capture gives `Q → B → M → B → final`.
The shared record supplies the compatibility that the preceding theorem needed
as a separate premise. `resume_step` connects this construction to the actual
raw resume and its ticket-discharge event; it retains the expression's checked
operand and assumes actual value closure.

Local theorems also preserve the result component through focus, plug, bind,
handler entry and return, clause return, and fresh resource entry. Cell return
derives the release access check from absence of the owner in the actual
returned value. Cleanup and application frames are not added as unchecked
pass-through cases.

`Examples.nested_results` proves this result component at all fourteen states
of the existing thirteen-step nested-clause execution. Capture steps use typed
requests and the actual handler clauses; the outer resume crosses a nonempty
ordinary prefix. It restores the caller's lexical result contract, consumes
the inner continuation, and reaches `17` with an empty stack. The earlier raw
trace and ownership ledger apply to these same states. The inner handler is
still installed after the outer ticket is consumed; this example does not
exercise two simultaneously live tickets. Negative checks reject a conflicting
historical answer and erasing a retained resource at the empty stack. Another
example accepts a scalar at a context whose saved input bound is `[7]`, without
changing that context's ordinary environment. The existing resource-owning
request also has a result certificate with actual checked handler clauses. Its
capture and resume retain the cell owner and waiting ordinary context.

The result registry in this module is a separate proof component. The following
construction joins its finite input records to the existing type/usage registry
and allocation history. The intermediate result certificates above, together
with the existing trace ledger, do not themselves establish intermediate joint
readiness. Callable contracts, request payload access, disposal and cleanup,
complete initial-term checking, whole-execution progress and formal Core
correspondence remain required. The unchanged
[Core fixture](fixtures/nested-handler-clause-result.ash) supplies endpoint
comparison evidence only. Multishot, escaping continuations and suspension
remain outside this target.

## Joint continuation records and ownership

[ClauseJoint.lean](ClauseJoint.lean) connects the retained result contracts to
the existing one-shot ownership, type/effect and usage judgments on the same
machine state. It tests whether those components can share one historical owner
record and survive the same capture and resume events. It adds no syntax or
runtime transition.

Each `TicketRecord` contains the existing joint continuation contract and
permissions, the result record `(Q,B)`, and a proof that `Q` is exactly the
canonical finite support of the continuation input port. `Registry.joint` and
`Registry.results` project the components from the same owner lookup. Their
insertion laws show that one allocation updates both projections together.
Answer support `B` remains independent of the answer's value type: a function
answer can retain resources that its port does not describe.

This record currently requires a finite continuation input bound. It therefore
cannot represent a callable continuation input whose port has unknown support.
That is a limitation of this proof checkpoint, not a proposed restriction on
one-shot Ash or a claim that every existing jointly valid state lifts to the
new judgment. Handler answers containing callable values are not excluded by
this record condition; checking callable behavior remains unfinished.

`Valid` combines the existing joint invariant with `ClauseFrames` result
checking for the same configuration, resource world and projected registry.
The joint invariant includes the ownership ledger, activation/name history,
live resource support, connected type/effect checking, one-shot usage, exact
ticket registry history and resource-name closure. `recorded_history` derives
that the combined and result registries describe exactly the historically
issued ticket owners. `registry_fresh` and `result_registry_fresh` therefore
derive both forms of absence from actual issued-owner freshness. Result-table
freshness is no longer an independent premise of the joined capture theorem.

`active_input_bound` links the live frame's actual input annotation to the
combined record and its result input bound. This is the common owner relation
needed by the independently checked components; the result projection cannot
silently choose a different input contract. `RegistryExtends` preserves every
existing record unchanged. Fresh insertion extends a registry, and extensions
compose, so historical metadata survives consumption and subsequent allocation.

`capture_preserves` follows the actual ordered handler cut. It uses current
operation typing and the selected handler's coverage to choose a clause, then
uses that same `ClauseAt`, operation output, owner, raw input annotation and
successor configuration for the effect/type and result constructions. The
handler-derived answer bound and the residual effect bound remain separate
fields. The theorem constructs one `NamedAccessStep`, one inserted combined
record, and the successor `Valid` judgment. Existing ownership and usage
preservation apply to that actual event. General outward payload access remains
a premise, as does fresh issued-owner allocation.

`empty_payload_access_checks` removes the access premise for an actual typed
request whose argument port has empty finite resource support. It derives the
operand's stored support from typing and value closure, then proves that this
support fits every selected outside stack. It uses the operation's argument
port, not its result port. Unknown callable support is never treated as empty.
The following declaration-boundary construction supplies that proof for
nonempty finite argument support in the represented declaration fragment.

`resume_preserves` derives actual value closure from current typing and the
access checks from the resume form. The retained result certificate supplies
the operand bound and shared-record recomposition proof; the existing joint
invariant supplies type/effect and one-shot authority. The same registry and
all components of `Valid` survive the actual ticket-discharge event. No saved
output/prefix compatibility premise is reintroduced.

Handler entry also preserves the combined judgment, with activation freshness
and the actual handler's effect instance, clauses and caller scope exposed.
Handler return and spent-clause return preserve it without extra access
premises. Cell return uses its retained result certificate to derive the actual
release exclusion, then preserves the ownership ledger together with type,
usage and result checks. `initial_configuration_valid` constructs an initial
combined certificate from the independent ordinary typing, one-shot usage,
resource-support and clause-result checks; it is not complete initial-term
checking or a decision procedure.

`CertifiedSteps` records `Valid` at every state of an existing named access
execution and requires a registry extension at every step. Its projections
recover the machine execution, final invariant and preservation of all old
records. The constructors require intermediate validity certificates; the
concrete example supplies them using the step theorems. This is not general
execution preservation derived solely from initial validity, or a theorem that
every valid state can take a step.

The concrete example starts with an ordinary checked handler program. Its five
steps enter the handler, capture ticket `5`, resume with `17`, return through
the handler and leave the spent clause boundary. Every state has the combined
certificate, and the final ledger records ticket `5` as issued and consumed
once. This example has no cell; the following boundary example exercises
capture and release of a resource owner with the combined invariant. The historical
record remains. A negative theorem rejects a new resume
of that consumed ticket on an empty stack despite the retained record. Another
negative theorem shows that a callable input cannot be supplied with a fictitious
finite bound. The [matching Core fixture](fixtures/single-handler-joint-result.ash)
returns `17 : Int`; this is endpoint comparison, not formal translation or
simulation.

This checkpoint establishes joint capture/resume preservation under the stated
finite input and payload conditions. It does not join every machine transition
or provide closing interfaces, and `Valid` must not be read as full `Ready`.
General payload access, callable input and behavior contracts, disposal and
cleanup, complete initial-term checking, whole-execution progress and formal
Core correspondence remain required. Multishot, escaping continuations and
suspension remain separate targets.

## Declared payloads across capture boundaries

[PayloadBoundary.lean](PayloadBoundary.lean) derives the capture access check
from the current structural judgments. Its scope is the represented
resource-parameter declarations and finite operation argument ports. The
question is whether a nonempty payload can safely pass a captured resource
scope without assuming the required outside-support inclusion as a premise.

`parameter_environment_range` proves that every identity produced by positional
parameter lookup occurs in the actual argument vector. It does not require
injective arguments: two parameters may refer to the same resource.
`realized_declared_support` then combines this range property with structural
type realization and the declaration rule excluding undeclared names and
runtime activation atoms. `declared_operation_resources` transports the result
through port erasure.

`signature_resources` connects these facts to actual compiled lookup. Both the
input and output ports of a selected operation mention only identities from
the exact requested effect instance. The proof covers the sealed cell read and
write signatures separately and validates user declarations, operation positions
and argument binding before using realization. It applies to this compiled
signature, not an arbitrary signature or the unrepresented parts of Core's
declaration system. A negative example rejects a declaration with a hidden
runtime resource atom.

Declared port resources do not describe every stored callable capture.
`typed_payload_bound` therefore retains the finite `PortBound` premise. It
recovers the first-order port shape and uses actual closed-value typing to bound
the operand's stored resources. No unknown support is replaced with an empty
set, and the operation's output bound is not used to justify its argument.

The selected handler's existing support theorem places its access dependencies
within the actual outside tail. Those dependencies include the resources of
its exact effect instance. `payload_crosses_selected_handler` composes the
following inclusions:

```text
actual operand resources
  ⊆ declared argument-port resources
  ⊆ requested effect-instance resources
  ⊆ selected handler access
  ⊆ outside-tail visibility ∪ ambient resources
```

The actual `HandlerCut` fixes this outside tail and the interpretation order.
The proof does not commute frames, treat all live resources as outside, or
assume that a captured owner remains available to the clause merely because
it appears in issued history.

`current_payload_access` obtains the finite argument contract from the current
combined state. Actual request typing and the selected handler's coverage
choose a clause; the retained `ClausesDerive` certificate supplies that clause's
finite input bound. Both lookups are equated before the support chain is used.
Thus the finite-bound premise comes from the actual checked handler, rather
than an extra boundary annotation supplied by a caller.

`request_access_checks` derives all current access obligations for an operation
expression. Its capture field applies the preceding theorem to each actual
cut; value-return and discard fields are excluded by the expression form.
For an unevaluated operand, the capture field is conditional on actual value
closure, as in the existing machine. This is not a new evaluation rule.
`capture_without_payload_premise` then constructs the same named capture,
combined record extension and successor `Valid` judgment as `ClauseJoint`,
without an `AccessChecks` premise. Fresh issued-owner allocation and actual
value form remain required.

The resource example starts at a fully checked runtime request with outer cell
`7` and inner cell `9` already owned. An exact `Carry<7>` handler sits between
them. The operand is a handle to cell `7`, so its support is nonempty. Capture
moves the inner cell and selected handler into ticket `5`; the outer cell stays
in the outside tail. The clause resumes with `17`, normal return releases cell
`9`, handler and clause returns restore the outside continuation, and normal
return releases cell `7`.

`resource_capture_release_execution` supplies combined validity at every state
of these six actual named steps, including record-preserving extensions.
`resource_capture_final_ledger` records the two resources and ticket as issued
and completed exactly once. Completion history is newest-first: `[resource 7,
resource 9, ticket 5]`. The example proves normal release after resume, not
abandonment through discard or cleanup hooks. It constructs the starting
runtime invariant directly; acquisition from an initial calculus term remains
a separate integration obligation.

The negative `captured_inner_handle_rejected` substitutes the inner handle
into the same `Carry<7>` request. The derived outside-support requirement would
place resource `9` in the tail that exposes only resource `7`, so no combined
`Valid` certificate can exist. This request also has an ordinary port mismatch:
`Carry<7>` declares a handle to `7`, not to `9`. The negative therefore does
not isolate escape checking from ordinary typing. Another example preserves
aliasing of two resource parameters. These cases distinguish actual owner identity from the
mere presence of a resource in the current world.

The [Core fixture](fixtures/outer-handle-capture-payload.ash) includes both
acquisitions and returns `17 : Int`. Its handler passes the outer handle while
capturing the inner scope. This is a concrete behavior comparison, not a formal
translation of acquisition or a Core simulation.

The capture payload premise is now derived for this finite-port declaration
fragment, including nonempty payloads. Callable payloads remain outside that
result because their ports do not bound actual captures. General callable
contracts, disposal/cleanup and closing interfaces, preservation through all
remaining computation forms, complete initial-term checking, whole-execution
progress and formal Core correspondence remain required. Multishot, escaping
continuations and suspension remain separate targets.

## Evaluated request and resume progress

[ClauseProgress.lean](ClauseProgress.lean) proves current-state progress for
evaluated requests and resumes under `ClauseJoint.Valid`. These theorems
preserve the combined result certificate and the same ownership, name,
support, type/effect, usage and registry-history invariant. They require no
additional access check or closing interface.

For an operation with a value operand, `request_progress` inspects the actual
ordered stack resolution:

- An absent interpreter requires the requested instance in the outgoing row.
- A selected builtin performs the actual nearest-cell read or write. The cell
  update preserves retained result frames, including their saved lexical
  contracts and handler-clause certificates. The registry stays unchanged.
- A selected source handler supplies its actual capture cut. Issued-owner
  uniqueness supplies a fresh ticket. The declared-payload theorem supplies
  access, and capture constructs one successor with all combined checks. The
  extended registry preserves every old record.

The theorem does not give builtins priority over handlers. It follows
`stack.erase.resolve` for either target. `interpreted_request_progress`
eliminates the outward alternative when that resolution succeeds;
`closed_request_progress` eliminates it when the outgoing row is empty.

For a value-operand resume, `resume_progress` derives lexical ticket resolution
from the current usage demand. Accessible-ticket membership locates an actual
live boundary in the same stack. The combined resume theorem then restores
the saved capture and complete intervening prefix, consumes the ticket, and
preserves the same historical registry. The caller supplies neither a cut nor
a separately asserted live owner.

These results remove the explicit local access and boundary premises from
these two progress cases in the finite-port fragment. The following proof
joins the remaining current forms admitted by the result rules and constructs
repeatable progress from the combined invariant. Callable application,
disposal/cleanup, full initial admission and full one-shot execution safety remain
open. The later `CheckedEvents` layer establishes finite checked-run preservation
for the current result fragment. Core correspondence remains an assessment of evidence, gaps and
mismatches; alignment changes are outside the current work.

## Repeatable progress for the current result fragment

[ClauseExecution.lean](ClauseExecution.lean) joins all current expression forms
admitted by `ClauseResults.Derives`. `current_progress` takes only the combined
`ClauseJoint.Valid` judgment. It proves one of three outcomes: a value with
empty control; an evaluated request with no selected interpreter that is
explicitly allowed by the outgoing row; or an actual `NamedAccessStep` whose
successor retains combined validity and every historical registry record.
`closed_progress` excludes the outward outcome for an empty outgoing row.

The covered forms are values, focus and return through ordinary contexts,
sequencing, branches, requests, handler installation and return, resume,
fresh resource entry and cell return. Application, `discard` and cleanup have
no rule in the current result judgment. `supported_head` derives their
exclusion from that judgment, rather than declaring them successful or adding
failure outcomes. Callable values may still be stored or returned; callable
application contracts remain unfinished.

For a current value, retained result bounds derive cell-release access. For a
focused expression, the focus proof excludes an already evaluated request.
Other ordinary heads cannot be requests. These facts construct the temporary
`NoSourceRequest` boundary used by non-capture result transport. That boundary
need not survive a step and is not a premise of the public progress theorem:
the successor's combined invariant suffices to reclassify its current form.
Source capture instead uses the declaration-derived payload proof and inserts
the same combined record used by its typing and usage checks.

`raw_preserves_results` transports result certificates through every
non-capture transition possible under the current result rules. It includes
handler entry, resume and fresh resource opening. It keeps the same result
registry and extends the resource world only when the actual event allocates
a resource. `join_non_capture` combines this result with the joint certificate
constructed for that same named event; it does not assume a successor in the
public admission or progress interface.

`initial_progress` starts from independent initial typing, usage, empty runtime
resource support, and a structural result derivation. `finite_prefix` proves
more than a first step: for every finite budget, one current combined invariant
constructs a certified execution that either uses the budget or terminates
earlier. A single `CertifiedPrefix` indexes the actual sequence by its length
and retains every intermediate invariant and registry extension. Its
`prefix_counted` and `prefix_certified` projections therefore concern the same
sequence, rather than unrelated paths between equal endpoints. `CountedSteps`
only counts existing named steps. The proof obtains each successor certificate
from progress; it does not ask the caller to certify future states.
`initial_finite_prefix` obtains the initial invariant from those four initial
premises.

At a terminal configuration, `terminal_accounting` proves that completed owners
are a permutation of issued owners and contain no duplicate. This accounts for
all owners recorded by that execution; ambient resources are not claimed to
have been acquired or released by it. `terminal_result_support` bounds actual
returned resource references by the admitted result bound. It does not claim
that an arbitrary ambient or result bound is empty.

This establishes repeatable progress and arbitrarily long safe prefixes for
the currently admitted fragment. It does not establish termination, admission
for callable application or disposal/cleanup, a complete executable checker,
or preservation for every arbitrary raw annotation choice. The full one-shot
target still needs those admission extensions and the appropriate universal
execution-safety theorem. Core correspondence remains an assessment; no Core
alignment work is included.

## Checking the supplied capture annotation

[CaptureAnnotations.lean](CaptureAnnotations.lean) addresses the quantifier
gap between constructing a valid capture and preserving validity for a
supplied capture event. The raw machine accepts any `Ty` as the new live
continuation's input annotation. That choice does not affect its ownership
transfer, but it constrains later typing. Raw ownership preservation therefore
does not imply type preservation for every annotation choice.

The counterexample starts from the combined-valid outer-handle request used
above. Its declared operation returns `Int`, and the selected clause resumes
with `17`. A raw capture can instead store `Unit` as the new continuation input.
The exact named event satisfies freshness and derived access checks and
preserves the ownership ledger. Its successor cannot be port-typed under any
ticket-signature registry: the live boundary requires a unit input while the
resume operand is an integer. Consequently no combined registry makes that
successor valid. This is a proof-model annotation counterexample; it is not
evidence that current Core accepts this mismatch.

`DeclaredCapture` adds one local declaration lookup to the existing capture
constructor. It retains the actual ordered cut, selected clause, operand and
owner, and requires the erased input annotation to equal the operation's
declared result port. Its other premises are the raw constructor's closure
and clause-substitution readiness checks. No premise asks for a successor
invariant, result certificate or access check. `declared_capture_executes`
projects directly to that same raw event; the judgment adds no machine step.
The example's matching integer annotation has a `DeclaredCapture` derivation;
its mismatched unit annotation has none.

`clause_selection_unique` proves that two selections of the same operation in
the same clause list choose identical parameter, continuation binder and body.
The existing pass constructor excludes matching keys, so this result does not
require an additional uniqueness premise. The selected retained result clauses
supply a finite output bound. `first_order_annotation` and `finite_annotation`
then prove that any raw annotation erasing to this finite port is its canonical
embedding. This argument does not extend to function ports with erased capture
metadata.

`selected_capture_preserves` uses those equalities to identify the supplied
event with the one for which capture construction establishes the combined
invariant. `declared_capture_preserves` quantifies over every
`DeclaredCapture` witness from a combined-valid state with a fresh owner.
It preserves the exact supplied successor and extends the historical registry
without changing any old record. Payload access remains derived from the
declarations and retained clauses.

This closes the annotation-preservation obligation for capture in the current
finite-port fragment. It does not establish universal execution safety across
other annotation-producing events. The following construction checks focus,
handler and resource annotations and derives them from current typing.
Callable application and disposal/cleanup admission
remain separate requirements. The counterexample rules out stating the full
target as preservation for unrestricted raw annotation choices; a universal
theorem must quantify over the correctly annotated executions and establish
how those annotations arise from initial checking.

## Checking supplied entry annotations

[EntryAnnotations.lean](EntryAnnotations.lean) covers focus frames, handler
answers and resource answers. `EntryTyping` is a structural judgment on the
supplied event. Its premises inspect code and continuation components already
present before the step:

- Focus checks the current child and its context at the supplied input/output
  ports, with the saved lexical ticket scope. The existing tail accepts the
  context's output and provides its effect row.
- Handler entry checks the current handler expression at the supplied answer
  port, and the existing tail at that port and its outward effect interface.
- Resource entry checks the current resource expression at the supplied
  answer port, with matching existing tail interfaces. The body is checked
  under every fresh opening by the expression typing rule.

None of these premises contains successor configuration typing, combined
validity or a promised execution. `entry_executes` projects the checked
constructor to the exact existing raw event. `entry_effects` derives its
successor's type and effect interfaces. For resource entry it uses the supplied
fresh activation, derives result/effect exclusion, and transports the current
and retained typing into the enlarged resource world. It does not substitute
a different activation to obtain the proof.

`entry_preserves` adds the current combined invariant and ordinary allocation
freshness. It derives access, preserves ownership, name history, usage and
resource-name closure, and transports the result certificate on the same
named step. These entries allocate no continuation ticket, so the entire
combined registry stays unchanged. Pending ticket translations remain checked
by the actual `PlainData` and usage rules; they are not replaced by new
annotations in this theorem.

The three annotation-existence theorems derive an `EntryTyping` witness from
the current type/effect configuration. Focus obtains its ports and pending
translation by typed context decomposition. Handler and resource entry choose
canonical embeddings of the current expression's result port. The handler
activation and resource identity may be supplied independently; execution
still checks their freshness. These construction results establish that the
annotation judgment adds no new admission requirement for those typed current
forms.

Together with `DeclaredCapture`, these rules cover annotation-producing events
admitted by the current result fragment. The following layer composes them with
annotation-free events into finite checked-run preservation. This does
not extend result admission to callable application, disposal or cleanup, and
does not change or prove correspondence with Core.

## Supplied capture records and finite checked runs

[CaptureRecords.lean](CaptureRecords.lean) makes the chosen continuation record
part of the checked capture. An existential record after each step is insufficient
for a supplied run: a later entry could have been checked against a different
record. `CheckedCapture` instead relates the actual selected operation, clause
and cut to one supplied record. Its type, effect and result-bound premises inspect
the current handler, saved segment and outside tail. They contain no successor
validity or successor-typing premise.

`checked_capture_exists` constructs such a record from current combined validity
and a declaration-checked capture. `checked_capture_preserves` proves combined
validity for that exact capture and that exact record insertion. The record
contains the finite declared continuation input, handler answer, residual effect
interface, result bounds and independently supplied ticket policy. Choosing
result metadata does not grant new ticket permissions.

[CheckedEvents.lean](CheckedEvents.lean) combines annotation-free events,
`EntryTyping` and `CheckedCapture`. A `CheckedEvent` specifies both the raw event
and its exact registry update. Stable events and entries keep the registry;
capture inserts its checked record. `CheckedStep` adds the existing owner and
handler-activation freshness conditions. `CheckedRun` composes those steps with
the same registry at each shared endpoint. Neither judgment assumes current,
intermediate or final combined validity, and neither assumes access checks.

`run_certified` derives the intermediate certificates along the supplied run
from one initial `ClauseJoint.Valid` premise. `run_preserves` therefore proves,
for every finite checked run, actual named access-checked execution, final
combined validity and preservation of historical records. The statement is
universal over checked runs; it does not select a different run or different
capture records to obtain preservation. The checks remain proof judgments,
not a complete executable annotation checker.

For an empty outgoing effect row, `run_closed_progress` proves that the endpoint
is terminal or has an actual invariant-preserving next event. Its conclusion is
a named event, not a `CheckedStep` witness. The following `CheckedProgress`
layer discharges the separate coverage obligation for checked continuations. At terminal endpoints,
`run_terminal_accounting` accounts for every issued owner exactly once, and
`run_terminal_result_support` bounds the returned value's resource dependencies.

This establishes finite checked-run preservation for the current result fragment.
It does not admit callable application, disposal or cleanup, prove termination,
or establish correspondence with validated Core. Full initial-term admission
and the complete one-shot safety target remain open. Core correspondence stays
an assessment of agreement and gaps; no Core alignment is performed.

## Progress extending the checked run

[CheckedProgress.lean](CheckedProgress.lean) constructs a checked next event
from current `ClauseJoint.Valid`. The judgment supplies types, effect interfaces,
usage, result bounds, ownership and name history. The theorem requires no
